title: A bedtime-story maker that writes like a picture book, not like a chatbot
summary: Five decisions that separate it from asking a chatbot for a bedtime story.

labels.research: What a raw chatbot gets wrong

problem: A parent at bedtime who wants a new story for a 3–5 year old: worth reading aloud tonight, and worth keeping if it's good.
research: Plots wander and end in a moral lecture.
No read-aloud rhythm: nothing a child can chant along to.
It drifts toward imitating famous books.
There is nowhere to keep the good ones.
did: The craft brief is built in, not left to the visitor: a rule of three, a chantable refrain, dramatic irony, wrong help before right help, a twist, an originality rule and a self-check.
The output is shaped for reading aloud: 12–14 spreads with illustration and read-aloud notes, a "Talk about it" question, and a full-screen reading mode.
It runs on the reader's own Claude account. A static site can't hide an API key, and I rejected a proxy holding my own key: cost and abuse handling for a side project.
Two shelves, with different privacy. Papa's shelf is public and curated by me; each visitor's stories stay in their own browser. A story with a child's name never goes public automatically.
owned: The shelf could hang on "Opening the shelf…". Loading no longer waits on the owner check, and an 8-second fallback shows an error code instead of a spinner forever.

title: A strategy tool that has to argue its move, not a chatbot in costume
summary: Three rounds of evals turned a pep talk with Sanskrit labels into a note that argues its lever.

labels.research: What a raw chatbot gets wrong

problem: Someone stuck on a real call at work (a turf war, a vendor's price hike, a favour asked by a skip-level) who wants one move they can make this week, not a list of considerations.
research: It gives a menu of options instead of one move.
Persona bots put invented quotes in Chanakya's mouth. Most viral "Chanakya" quotes aren't in the Arthashastra at all.
It cites sources it can't back up.
It will happily borrow the text's darker tactics: spies, leaks, planted rumours.
did: Verified sources only: the Arthashastra in Shamasastry's 1915 translation, four Panchatantra books, three Thirukkural chapters, and operator frameworks checked against Lenny's Podcast transcripts. Five claims I couldn't find in the transcripts were cut.
The model can't write a citation. It returns a short ID; the page maps it from a fixed list and drops anything else, so a made-up reference never reaches the screen.
One move, and it has to argue its lever: who has to change, how strong they are relative to you, and whether you want the same thing.
"Where this tool stops": the Arthashastra endorses spies and poison. The tool keeps the strategy, refuses those tactics, and says why.
Two model sizes on the visitor's own Claude account: a fast one asks up to four questions, a stronger one writes the note.
I narrowed a claim. The subtitle said "tested against modern operators"; the eval showed that layer was decoration, so the claim went.
owned: Round 1 of evals (20 situations): 15 of 18 notes picked conciliation, which was generic advice wearing Sanskrit labels, and all 18 "your ground" sections cited the identical set of sources, copied from the example in my own prompt. Round 2 fixed both, then overcorrected: the tool started labelling the visitor's own team and a supportive manager as rivals. Round 3 fixed the labels and brought the fables back where they fit. What's still open is listed on the tool as known limits, and the next round adds external, adversarial cases.

title: A one-thumb game for the minute you're stuck in traffic
summary: One prompt gets you a lane-dodging game. It doesn't get you a reason to come back tomorrow.

labels.research: What a raw chatbot gets wrong

problem: Anyone with a phone and 60 seconds to kill: no sign-in, no tutorial, playing within a tap.
research: No guarantee a run is fair.
No road that feels like the one you're actually stuck on.
did: Road of the day: everyone gets the same seeded road, changing at midnight IST. Shared roads make scores comparable and give a reason to return.
One lane is always open, so every crash is the player's fault, never the game's. Fairness is what makes "one more go" feel earned.
A streak with a one-day grace: a habit without punishment. No ads, no sign-in, no nagging.
Wordle-style sharing (🟨 clean / 🟥 hit per 200 m). The share text is the distribution plan.
Unlimited retries; the share shows the latest run. Generosity over a strict one-attempt rule, for now.
Low floor, high ceiling: speed and hazards ramp up over a run, and each road has its own landmarks and hazard mix.
